Prologue

2080

The door to the scan room weighed nine hundred pounds, and in wet weather it stuck.

She had meant to put in a work order about it for three years. Instead she had learned exactly where to put her shoulder, high and near the copper seam, with her weight coming off the back foot. She put it there now, and the door sighed on its gaskets and let her through.

"Sounds like a bank vault," said the man on the table.

"It sort of is."

"What are you keeping in?"

"Nothing in. Everything out." She settled the coil over his lower back and tucked the foam wedge under his knees. "Your phone, the radios, the lift motors, the ambulances out on the ramp. The magnet hears all of it, and it ruins the pictures."

He was a retired roofer with two bad discs and a wife waiting in the cafeteria, and he had told her all of that in the first four minutes. People talked like that when they were afraid of the tube. She had been running scans in this basement for sixteen years, and she liked the talkers. You could give a talker something to do.

"Twenty-two minutes," she said. "It's going to knock. Count the knocks if you want."

"How many are there?"

"Nobody's ever finished counting."

He laughed, and she slid him in.

The control room had one window that was not a screen, a slot of wired glass set high in the outside wall at the level of the ambulance ramp. Mostly it showed tires.

At 10:14 it went white.

It was not bright but white, as if someone had pressed a sheet of paper against the glass. She looked up from the console while the sequence ran and the knocking went on through the wall, steady as a heartbeat. The white faded back to grey morning, and she thought lightning and waited for thunder.

None came, and she was still waiting when the glass went white again.

The resident in the reading chair had seen it too. He was young, three months into the rotation, and he took off his glasses as if they were the problem. "That's high up," he said. "That's a lot of high up."

In the scan room the magnet kept knocking, the control room lights stayed on, and the console went on humming to itself. Nothing inside the wing so much as flickered.

That was what made her get up.

She went down the corridor to the wing's outer door, which was steel and copper and hung on hinges as thick as her wrist, with a red manual release lever that she had been told in training never to touch. The little panel of glass in it looked out on the main hospital. Normally it showed a bright hallway, a vending machine, people with lanyards.

Now the hallway beyond it was dark.

She put her shoulder to the door and went through.

The quiet was the first thing, because a hospital was never quiet. It had a hum under everything, pumps and fans and a hundred monitors ticking over, and you stopped hearing it after a week. She heard it now by its absence. The wall clock over the vending machine said 10:14 and its second hand did not move. Her locker was ten steps away, and when she opened it and took out her phone, the screen stayed black no matter what she pressed.

Out on the ramp an ambulance had rolled backward into a concrete post and stopped there with its doors open, and nobody was in it.

She understood then, because her whole job was keeping stray fields out of one room, and she knew what a big enough pulse did to anything with a wire in it. She had simply never imagined the room would be the thing that was left.

A woman came down the stairwell in the dark with one hand on the rail. It was the charge nurse from the fourth floor, still in blue scrubs, who had once lent her a pen and never asked for it back.

"Is your power on?"

"Yes."

"I have eleven people on ventilators," the nurse said, "and every one of them is dead. I have everyone who can walk squeezing a bag by hand. How many can you take?"

She did the arithmetic out loud, so that later nobody could say she hadn't. The wing ran on an isolated battery bank and a diesel generator in a shielded vault, because the magnet's cooling could never be allowed to stop. The inverter could carry the magnet and the lights and only so much else. If she shut down the second scanner and the reading room, she could free up a line of protected outlets.

"Eight," she said. "Eight ventilators. And the fuel goes from three days to about thirty hours."

The nurse closed her eyes for exactly one second.

"Eight," she said, and turned back up the stairs.

The resident had followed her out. "If we open that door and there's a third one," he said, "we lose everything in here. The magnet. The generator. All of it."

"I know."

"We don't know it's over."

"No," she said. "We don't."

She went back for the roofer. She stopped the scan at minute nine and slid him out, and he blinked up at her from the table.

"We'll finish it later," she said.

They never did.

"What's happening?"

"I need hands."

He looked at her face for a moment, and then he sat up with a sound through his teeth for the discs, and got off the table. "Where do you want them?"

She pulled the red lever, and the outer door unlatched with a sound like a dropped wrench. She wedged it with a sandbag from the magnet room and went up four flights in the dark behind the nurse.

They brought them down on bedsheets. Four people on the corners, one walking alongside squeezing the bag, a sixth ahead with a hand on the rail calling out the landings. The roofer took a corner every trip. The resident took a corner every trip after the first. She lost count of the stairs and then stopped trying.

By evening there were eight machines hissing along her corridor, plugged into the orange outlets. Past them, near the door, there were three more beds. People sat beside those beds in turns, squeezing a bag every five seconds, handing it on when their fingers cramped.

The roofer was sitting beside the last one, and he did not look up when she passed.

She walked up the ramp into the dark.

There was no light anywhere. Not in the towers downtown, not on the bridge, not in the long rows of houses across the river where her husband had driven that morning at a quarter to ten. No cars moved and no planes crossed. Far off to the east, a thread of smoke went up from where something had come down out of the sky.

Behind her, one corridor glowed through the propped door, the only lit thing she could see.

The resident came up beside her. "They'll have it back by morning," he said.

She did not answer, because she was thinking about who they were. Everyone who knew how to turn it back on was standing in the dark somewhere, waiting for someone else to do it.

She went back down and found the generator log on its clipboard. She wrote the time from the wing clock, because it was the only clock in the city that still knew it. Under it she wrote the fuel.

Then she ruled a new line and sat down beside the nearest bed and took the bag.

2090

The boy carried the battery trays because he liked to. She let him because her back no longer did.

"This one's the grumpy one," he said, setting it on the bench.

"They don't have moods."

"This one does. It's lower than the others every morning. It's sulking."

She checked it, and it was lower than the others. "It's got a bad cell."

"That's what sulking is," he said, pleased.

It was day 3,641 by her log, and nobody else kept the count anymore. Outside, the car park was bean rows and sunflowers for the oil press, and the fence was built of bed frames and ambulance doors. The generator ran on pressed sunflower oil now, and it complained about it. The magnet still ran too, cold and patient, one afternoon a week, for whoever the charge nurse decided needed it most.

Everything was whoever-needed-it-most now.

Twice in ten years people had come up the road with a working truck and a plan to bring the grid back. Twice they had gone away again. The resident had died in the third winter from a cut on his hand. The roofer had built the fence and lived to see it finished. On the fifth day after the lights went out, she had walked across the river bridge and back, and she had never walked it again.

The boy had come in on that first night, three years old, asleep on a stack of lead aprons. Somebody's. By the time anyone had worked out whose, there was nobody to give him back to. Now he was thirteen, all elbows, and he wanted to know what every dial in the wing was for.

The survey meter sat on the bench in its open drawer. It was for checking the old isotope store, and it had not had anything to say in years.

It started to click.

She looked at it. The boy looked at it.

"Is it broken?"

"It doesn't break." She picked it up and turned it slowly. The clicking thinned toward the south wall and thickened toward the north. It climbed as she watched until the clicks ran together into a sound like rain on a roof.

Down the corridor, a small amber light came on over the magnet room door. It was the field monitor, and she had not seen it lit since before the boy could walk.

"Is that the magnet?"

"The magnet doesn't do that."

Her ears popped, and somewhere outside a dog started barking and would not stop.

"Smells like a struck match," the boy said.

She put down the meter and picked up the pry bar she used on the battery terminals. "Stay behind me."

The north lot was the bean field now, and four of the little ones were down between the frames with a basket. The man who kept the goats was mending the frame at the end of the row.

Beside the last frame, the air was split.

That was the only word she had for it. A line hung upright in the air, taller than a man, like a crack in a window where there was no window. The beans behind it bent wrong, and the wind, which had come off the river all day, was blowing toward it now.

Something stepped out.

It was smaller than a man and the color of old newspaper. Its limbs were the wrong lengths for each other. Where a face belonged there was only more of the same dry skin.

It did not look around but came straight down the row toward the children, and when it reached the bean frame it did not go around. It went through, and the frame went flat.

"Ramp!" she shouted. "Now! Run!"

The little ones ran, and the smallest fell in the dirt and got up crying.

The goat man drove his pitchfork into its side. The tines went in to the shank, and the thing did not even turn its head. It kept walking and dragged him three steps before the handle tore out of his hands.

She swung the pry bar at its head with both arms. It was like hitting a sack of wet sand, and the shock went up both arms into her shoulders. The thing turned toward her, and she stepped back, and her heel caught the fallen frame.

She went down hard on her back. The smallest child was on the ground behind her, still crying, not running anymore.

The thing came on.

Then the boy was in front of her.

He did not have a tool. He did not have anything. He put both arms up with his palms out, the way you catch a door that is swinging at your face, and he shouted something that was not a word.

The air in front of his hands changed.

She saw it the way you see heat over a stove: a bend in the light, curved like the side of a bowl, wide enough to cover him and her and the child behind her. There was a faint shine along its edge, like the surface of water seen from underneath.

The thing hit it at a walk, and stopped.

It did not bounce. It stopped the way a loaded cart stops against a wall, all at once, with the dust jolting off it. It leaned in and pushed, and the boy's heels slid back and cut two grooves in the dirt.

She counted, because she had counted everything for ten years.

One.

Its back was stretched long with the effort. She had looked inside ten thousand bodies, and she knew where a shoulder should hinge. This one did not. It was simply held there, pinched together like a wet paper bag holding its shape.

Two. She got up.

Three. "The fork!" she shouted. "Hook the other side!"

Four. She drove the flat end of the pry bar into the pinch at the shoulder.

Five. She leaned her whole weight on it. The goat man had his fork back and caught the far side under the arm.

Six. The boy made a sound like someone lifting too much, and blood ran out of his nose.

Seven. The shoulder tore, not like meat but like old canvas splitting, and grey dust puffed out of the seam.

Eight. They pulled it over together, and it never reached the ground. There was no body, only a grey slump in the dirt and a haze hanging in the air.

The bend in the air went out like a breath.

The boy sat down in the dirt.

She got to him on her knees. His hands were white and cold as creek stones, and he was shaking so hard his teeth clicked. The front of his shirt was red.

"Did I—" he said.

"Yes."

"What did I do?"

She held his cold hands in hers and told him the truth.

"I don't know."

When she looked up for the split in the air, it was gone, and the beans behind it were only beans.

The grey stuff looked like ash from a stove. The wind was still blowing across the lot, and the ash lay in it and did not lift.

It moved anyway. It ran, slow and grey, across the old asphalt toward the drain grate. She had watched contrast dye move through a vein like that, feeling for the path. It gathered in the cracks and thickened there, and took on a dull shine.

She brought the survey meter out, and it clicked faster over the ash than it had over anything in ten years.

She did not know what the ash was, but she knew the meter wanted it, and ten years had taught her to keep anything a working instrument had an opinion about. So she sent for specimen jars and a spatula, and she scraped the cracks clean on her knees, and she screwed the lids down tight.

The boy slept fourteen hours in the corridor where the ventilators had once stood. She sat beside him with two fingers on his wrist while his pulse went fast, then slow, then steady. His hands stayed cold until morning.

The magnet's monitor had printed a spike at 3:52 in the afternoon. The meter had counted until its needle pinned, and between them the machines had noticed everything.

None of them had noticed a thirteen-year-old boy put his hands up.

In the morning she took down the log, which was on its fourteenth volume. It had never skipped a day, not the fever winter, not the winter the resident died. It had always been for two things: what was left, and what it cost.

She wrote:

Day 3,641. North lot. 3:52 p.m.

Survey meter reading with no source, approx. ten minutes before. Field monitor alarm. Air split upright near the bean frames, taller than a man. Closed without anyone closing it.

One animal came through. Not an animal. No bones that I could find. Fork did not stop it. Bar did not stop it. Came apart when levered at the shoulder seam. Left grey residue. Residue does not blow away. Meter reads it. Kept in jars one through four.

She wrote his name.

Age thirteen. Put both hands up. It stopped against something in the air in front of him. Visible, barely. Held approx. eight seconds. After: nosebleed, cold hands, tremor. Slept fourteen hours.

Nothing measured what he did.

She sat with the pencil for a long time, and then she wrote the last line, because the log was for what was left, and the question was all that was left.

Is he the only one?

Sixty years later.

Twenty-five days to Meridian.
